Two compression modes — here's when to use each

Quality Level is a single-pass compression. You pick a quality (low / medium / high), the tool renders each page at that quality as a JPEG, and you get your compressed PDF. Use this when you want to make a PDF smaller for email or general sharing and don't have a specific size target. Medium quality typically reduces scanned PDFs by 60–80% and photo-heavy PDFs by 50–70%. Text-only PDFs (converted from Word or generated by software) compress less — often 20–40% — because their content is already efficiently encoded as vectors, not bitmaps.

Target Size runs a binary search — it tries different combinations of JPEG quality (from 0.08 to 0.90) and render resolution (from 600px to 1600px page width) until it gets your PDF under the size you specified. Use this when a portal has a strict upload limit. Common limits: Passport Seva portal requires supporting documents under 1 MB. UPSC and many state government portals require documents under 300 KB or 500 KB. Company HR portals commonly cap resumes and certificates at 500 KB or 1 MB. Enter the exact limit and let the tool find the right settings — no manual trial and error.

The honest trade-off you should know about

This tool compresses PDFs by rendering each page to a canvas and re-saving it as a JPEG image. This is how browser-based compression works — and it has one consequence that matters depending on what you're doing: text in the output PDF is no longer selectable or searchable. The text is captured as pixels in an image, not as actual characters.

For most everyday uses — submitting to government portals, sharing via email or WhatsApp, printing — this doesn't matter. But if you need a compressed PDF where someone can still copy-paste text, highlight it, or search it, this tool isn't the right fit. In that case, use Adobe Acrobat (paid) or Ghostscript (free, command-line) which compress PDFs by removing duplicate resources and downsampling images while keeping text as actual text.

Why text-only PDFs compress less than scanned ones

A PDF generated from a Word document, spreadsheet, or presentation stores text as vector characters — tiny mathematical descriptions of letter shapes — and stores images separately. This format is already very compact. When this tool renders that page and re-saves it as a JPEG, it's converting something compact into a bitmap, which is actually less efficient for pure text.

Scanned PDFs are different: they already store each page as a photograph of a physical document. Re-compressing that photograph as a JPEG at lower quality removes image data that the human eye doesn't notice — so the file gets dramatically smaller. A 10 MB scanned document can often compress to under 1 MB at medium quality while looking completely readable on screen. That same compression on a text-generated PDF might only yield a 20–30% reduction.

Portal-specific file size requirements

If you're compressing for a specific portal, here are the actual limits commonly required (always verify on the portal itself, as these change):

  • Passport Seva (PSP): Supporting documents — 1 MB per file
  • UPSC DAF / application forms: Photo 300 KB, signature 20 KB, certificates 500 KB
  • IBPS / SBI bank exams: Photo 50–100 KB, documents 500 KB
  • JEE / NEET: Photo under 100 KB, documents under 500 KB
  • DigiLocker uploads: 10 MB per document (rarely an issue)
  • Income Tax portal (ITR documents): 5 MB per attachment

Use Target Size mode and enter the limit. The tool handles the rest.

Frequently asked questions

My PDF is 8 MB of scanned pages. What quality should I use?

Start with Medium quality. For a typical 8 MB scanned document, medium quality usually produces output in the 1–2 MB range while remaining clearly readable. If you need it smaller (under 500 KB), try Low quality — scanned text at low quality is still legible at normal viewing sizes, though it will look noticeably softer if zoomed in. If a specific portal has a limit, use Target Size mode instead and skip the manual testing.

Why didn't my PDF compress much?

Almost always this means your PDF was generated from a digital source (Word, Excel, PowerPoint, or a print-to-PDF from a website) rather than scanned. These PDFs store text as vectors, which this compression method doesn't reduce efficiently. You're also converting vector content to bitmaps, which can sometimes make the file slightly larger at high quality settings. Try Low quality to force more reduction, or use Target Size with your desired limit.

Can I compress the same PDF multiple times to make it smaller?

Compressing an already-compressed output will make the quality noticeably worse without a proportional size reduction. Each compression pass re-encodes the JPEG images at lower quality, introducing visible artifacts. If the first compression didn't hit your target, use Target Size mode on the original file instead of re-compressing the output.

Is my PDF safe to compress here?

Yes. The compression runs entirely inside your browser tab using PDF.js and pdf-lib. Your file is loaded into browser memory, processed there, and the output is downloaded directly to your device. Nothing is sent over the network. You can compress sensitive documents — medical reports, financial statements, legal files, government IDs — without any privacy concern.

What's the maximum file size I can compress?

There's no server-imposed limit because there's no server involved. The practical limit is your browser's available memory. Each page is rendered at full resolution before being re-encoded, which uses RAM proportional to the page dimensions. A 50 MB PDF with 100 pages will use significant memory — on a phone or older computer this may cause the tab to crash. For very large files, process them in chunks: split the PDF first, compress each part, then re-merge if needed.
